rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four usable lanes and tells them which ones are thin before a journalist has to. Its best line, "Selling to a second buyer without a sales team," identifies the real strategic tension without pretending the launch alone proves it. B has good bones, but "Linear is selling to the enterprise without an enterprise sales team" walks past the facts: the update says no enterprise sales team is mentioned, not that Linear is selling enterprise or has no sales motion.
gaps_in_A: "Linear opens the product-management market it spent years refusing to enter" invents motive and history. The update says Linear is expanding beyond engineering teams; it does not say the company refused this market for years.
"the competitive set is forced to react" overstates the launch. No competitor response is supplied, and A correctly refuses "Linear takes on Jira" later, so this line undercuts its own discipline.
"Stakeholder views are, by definition, for people who open the tool weekly, not hourly" is a plausible product-craft inference, not a supplied fact. It should be framed as a question, not a premise.
gaps_in_B: "Linear is selling to the enterprise without an enterprise sales team" is the big sin. The facts do not say enterprise, do not confirm no sales team, and do not describe the buyer as enterprise.

"Jira, Asana, Notion, and Monday" names a competitive set the update did not supply. Fine as reporter context only if labeled as beat context; here it slides into "incumbents own" and starts sounding like claimed market proof.

"designers, stakeholders) that historically wants visual roadmaps" imports behavior not in the update. The given facts say designers and stakeholder views, not that this audience historically wants visual roadmaps.
"cross-functional, multi-seat sale" is probably true in the real world, but it is not in the supplied facts. For this exercise, probably true is still how hallucinations dress for meetings.
